events.title: Hesse passes the world's first data protection law
events.place: Hessischer Landtag (Stadtschloss), Wiesbaden, Hesse, West Germany
events.summary: On 7 October 1970 the parliament of the West German state of Hesse passed the Datenschutzgesetz (GVBl. I S. 625), which came into force on 13 October 1970. It set rules for the processing of personal data by state authorities and bodies under state supervision, and created the office of a data protection commissioner to oversee them. The occasion was the introduction of automated data processing in the Hessian administration.
events.significance: The word and the institution of 'data protection' begin here: a statute written because government computers, not snoopers at the door, had become the threat.

sources.title: HHStAW Fonds 557: Der Hessische Datenschutzbeauftragte (fonds description)
sources.quote: Am 7. Oktober 1970 verabschiedete der Hessische Landtag das 'Datenschutzgesetz' (GVBl. I S. 625).
sources.note: Translation: 'On 7 October 1970 the Hessian Landtag passed the Data Protection Act (GVBl. I p. 625).' The same page gives entry into force as 13.10.1970, says the law covered state authorities and bodies under state supervision (§ 1), and names the introduction of automated data processing (ADV) in the state administration as the occasion. Page date is the last accession year listed (2018-2024).

sources.institution: Der Hessische Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit (HBDI)
sources.title: Geschichte des Datenschutzes
sources.quote: Das Hessische Datenschutzgesetz von 1970 war das erste Datenschutzgesetz deutschland- und weltweit. Es reagierte auf die zunehmende Automatisierung der Datenverarbeitung.
sources.note: Translation: 'The Hessian Data Protection Act of 1970 was the first data protection law in Germany and worldwide. It responded to the increasing automation of data processing.' Page undated; year approximate.

sources.institution: Der Landesbeauftragte für den Datenschutz und die Informationsfreiheit Baden-Württemberg
sources.title: 50 Jahre Datenschutz: In Hessen trat das weltweit erste Datenschutzgesetz in Kraft
sources.quote: Heute vor 50 Jahren, am 13.10.1970, trat das weltweit erste Datenschutzgesetz für die öffentliche Verwaltung in Kraft – und zwar in Hessen.
sources.note: Translation: 'Fifty years ago today, on 13.10.1970, the world's first data protection law for public administration came into force - in Hesse.'

events.locationNote: The Hessian Landtag sits in the former ducal Stadtschloss on Schlossplatz, Wiesbaden.

events.title: Willi Birkelbach becomes the first data protection commissioner
events.place: Hessischer Landtag (Stadtschloss), Wiesbaden, Hesse, West Germany
events.summary: On 8 June 1971 the Hessian Landtag, on the state government's proposal, elected Willi Birkelbach as Hesse's data protection commissioner, the office created by the 1970 act. The Hessian authority describes him as the world's first data protection commissioner. From the start, anyone who believed their data had been mishandled by a covered public body could appeal to the commissioner (§ 11 of the 1970 act).
events.significance: Data protection is born with an independent watchdog attached: a person, not just a rulebook, to whom individuals can complain.

sources.institution: Der Hessische Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit (HBDI)
sources.title: Geschichte des Datenschutzes
sources.quote: Der weltweit erste Datenschutzbeauftragte war Willi Birkelbach, der am 8. Juni 1971 vom Hessischen Landtag auf Vorschlag der Landesregierung gewählt wurde.
sources.note: Translation: 'The world's first data protection commissioner was Willi Birkelbach, who was elected by the Hessian Landtag on 8 June 1971 on the proposal of the state government.'

sources.title: HHStAW Fonds 557: Der Hessische Datenschutzbeauftragte (fonds description)
sources.quote: Bereits im Datenschutzgesetz von 1970 war das Recht aller Betroffenen auf Anrufung des Datenschutzbeauftragten enthalten (GVBl. I S. 625, § 11).
sources.note: Translation: 'The 1970 Data Protection Act already contained the right of all data subjects to appeal to the data protection commissioner (GVBl. I p. 625, § 11).'

events.title: US Fair Credit Reporting Act regulates the credit bureaus
events.summary: The Fair Credit Reporting Act was approved on 26 October 1970 as Title VI of Public Law 91-508, a statute whose earlier titles imposed record-keeping and currency-reporting duties on banks. It found a need to ensure that consumer reporting agencies act with 'a respect for the consumer's right to privacy', required them to adopt reasonable procedures for the confidentiality, accuracy, relevancy and proper use of information, and limited disclosure of consumer reports to purposes specified in the Act. The Federal Trade Commission enforces it.
events.significance: The first US law aimed at a private data industry, it treated a dossier compiled about a person as something that person could see, dispute and restrict.

sources.institution: U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo), United States Statutes at Large vol. 84
sources.title: Public Law 91-508, October 26, 1970, 84 Stat. 1114 (Title VI - Consumer Credit Reporting)
sources.quote: There is a need to insure that consumer reporting agencies exercise their grave responsibilities with fairness, impartiality, and a respect for the consumer's right to privacy.
sources.note: Section 602(a)(4) of the new Title VI. The scanned statute (OCR) also shows 'Approved October 26, 1970' and the Title VI effective date of 180 days after enactment; Titles I-II of the same public law are the bank record-keeping and currency-reporting provisions later known as the Bank Secrecy Act.

sources.title: Fair Credit Reporting Act (Legal Library: Statutes)
sources.quote: Information in a consumer report cannot be provided to anyone who does not have a purpose specified in the Act.
sources.note: The same page notes the Commission 'retains all its enforcement authority' after Dodd-Frank moved most rulemaking to the CFPB. Page undated; date is access year.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are the US Capitol, seat of the Congress that passed the act.

events.title: Sweden's Data Act: the first national data protection law
events.summary: Sweden's Datalag (SFS 1973:289) was issued on 11 May 1973 after the Riksdag adopted the government's bill that spring. It barred anyone from setting up or keeping a computerised personal register without the permission of a new authority, Datainspektionen (the Data Inspection Board), which was established from 1 July 1973; the permit provisions took effect a year later, after a constitutional amendment. The Liberal member of parliament Kerstin Anér was a leading advocate.
events.significance: The first nation-wide data protection law put a licensing regulator between every personal register and the people in it.

sources.title: Datalag (1973:289)
sources.note: 'Issued: 1973-05-11'. The page also records 'Upphävd: 1998-10-24' (repealed 24 October 1998). The statutory text shown is the consolidated version after later amendments (e.g. Lag 1982:446 split licence and permit), not the 1973 wording. Human-readable page: https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/svensk-forfattningssamling/datalag-1973289_sfs-1973-289/

sources.institution: Svensk Juristtidning (1979), p. 497 - Jan Freese, director-general of Datainspektionen
sources.title: Datainspektionen
sources.quote: I samband därmed beslöts att en särskild myndighet, datainspek tionen, skulle inrättas fr. o. m. den 1 juli 1973. Samtidigt trädde reglerna i datalagen om tillsyn över personregister i kraft. De bestämmelser som avser tillståndsfrågor trädde i kraft först ett år senare då grundlagsändring skett.
sources.note: Translation: 'At the same time it was decided that a special authority, the Data Inspection Board, would be established from 1 July 1973. At the same time the Data Act's rules on supervision of personal registers came into force. The provisions on permits came into force only a year later, once a constitutional amendment had been made.' The line-break hyphen in 'datainspek tionen' is as printed on the digitised page.

sources.title: Sverige blir först i världen med att införa en nationell datalag
sources.quote: Den drivande politikern, som i debatter och i riksdagsmotioner talar sig varm för behovet av att skydda medborgarnas personliga integritet, är folkpartisten Kerstin Anér.
sources.note: Translation: 'The driving politician, who argued warmly in debates and parliamentary motions for the need to protect citizens' personal integrity, was the Liberal Kerstin Anér.' The page also says the new Data Act provided that no personal register could be set up or kept without the Data Inspection Board's permission.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are the Riksdag building on Helgeandsholmen, Stockholm.

events.title: HEW report proposes a Code of Fair Information Practice
events.place: U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: In July 1973 the Secretary's Advisory Committee on Automated Personal Data Systems, chaired by the computer scientist Willis Ware, published 'Records, Computers and the Rights of Citizens' (DHEW Publication No. (OS) 73-94). It recommended a federal 'Code of Fair Information Practice' for all automated personal data systems, resting on five principles, beginning with 'There must be no personal data record keeping systems whose very existence is secret.' The committee also opposed a standard universal identifier and urged steps to curb the drift of the Social Security number toward becoming one.
events.significance: The founding text of the fair information practice principles - and it already said that in trading privacy for a benefit 'both parties to the exchange should participate in setting the terms'.

sources.institution: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE)
sources.title: Records, Computers and the Rights of Citizens (full text of the 1973 report)
sources.quote: Although there is nothing inherently unfair in trading some measure of privacy for a benefit, both parties to the exchange should participate in setting the terms.
sources.note: Summary and Recommendations section. The same page states: 'the report recommends the enactment of a Federal "Code of Fair Information Practice" for all automated personal data systems. The Code rests on five basic principles...' and that it 'opposes the establishment of such an identification scheme at this time.'

sources.institution: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Privacy and Civil Liberties
sources.title: Overview of the Privacy Act of 1974 (2020 edition): Introduction
sources.quote: To address these risks, the HEW Report developed what it called a “code of fair information practices,” now more commonly called the Fair Information Practice Principles, or FIPPs.
sources.note: Gives the full citation, DHEW Publication No. (OS) 73-94 (July 1973), and credits the FIPPs to committee chairman Willis Ware, executive director David B. H. Martin and associate director Carole Parsons. DOJ's own PDF of the report (justice.gov/opcl/docs/rec-com-rights.pdf) returned HTTP 401 to scripts.

events.locationNote: Approximate coordinates of HEW's headquarters on Independence Avenue SW, Washington, D.C. (today's Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building).

events.title: US Privacy Act puts fair information practices into federal law
events.summary: The Privacy Act of 1974 (Public Law 93-579, 88 Stat. 1896) was approved on 31 December 1974 and took effect on 27 September 1975 as the principal law governing how US federal agencies handle personal information. Congress passed it in the final week of the 93rd Congress, in the wake of Watergate and COINTELPRO, relying on the HEW report's code of fair information practices. President Gerald Ford's signing statement, released at Vail, Colorado, called it 'an historic beginning'; the act also created an advisory Privacy Protection Study Commission.
events.significance: The first national statute to codify the fair information practices - but only for the federal government, leaving the private sector to later, piecemeal laws.

sources.institution: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Privacy and Civil Liberties
sources.title: Overview of the Privacy Act of 1974 (2020 edition): Introduction
sources.quote: The Privacy Act of 1974, Pub Law No. 93-579, 88 Stat 1896 (Dec. 31, 1974), codified at 5 U.S.C. § 552a (2018), went into effect on September 27, 1975
sources.note: The same page: 'Enacted in the wake of the Watergate and the Counterintelligence Program (COINTELPRO) scandals' and 'The Act was passed in great haste during the final week of the Ninety-Third United States Congress.'

sources.institution: The American Presidency Project, University of California, Santa Barbara
sources.title: Gerald R. Ford, Statement on Signing the Privacy Act of 1974
sources.quote: The Privacy Act of 1974 signified an historic beginning by codifying fundamental principles to safeguard personal privacy in the collection and handling of recorded personal information by Federal agencies.
sources.note: Editorial note on the page: 'As enacted, S. 3418, approved December 31, 1974, is Public Law 93-579 (88 Stat. 1896). The statement was released at Vail, Colo.' Ford also refers to 'the [Privacy Protection Study] Commission created by this law'.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are the US Capitol (Congress). Ford's signing statement was released at Vail, Colorado.
